To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Fermi level at the semiconductor surface can be pinned by adsorbate induced gap states, 2) the adsorbate induced states can have a donor character, 3) the adsorbates that form metallic interfaces at the semiconductor surface are the ones with a high ionization energy, and 4) the adsorbation of the metallic adatoms at the semiconductor surface results in a Schottky barrier formation.

the Fermi level at a Ga-GaAs(1 10) interface is pinned at 0.5 eV above the valence band maximum, the Fermi level of a Mn-GaAs( 110) interface is pinned 0.5-0.7 eV above the VBM and the Fermi level in a Ca-GaAs (110) interface is 1.5-1.6 eV above the top of the valence band.
the pinning of Fermi level in the GaAs band gap occurs at the interface between GaAs and a variety of metals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of Schottky barriers on III-V compound semiconductors.
the electronic properties of metal-semiconductor interfaces and the formation of Schottky barriers.
the formation of Schottky barriers on n- and p-GaAs(100) and n-GaAs(111) surfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a metal-to-insulator transition is associated with the pinning of E _{F} at the semiconductor surface.
the pinning of E-F is associated with the formation of an interface metal.

the Fermi level pinning in metal-GaAs(111) interfaces is caused by the formation of gap states at low coverage, and the appearance of interface metallicity at high coverage, which is the consequence of a high density of metal-induced gap states.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a metallic character of the interface is a sufficient condition for Fermi level pinning at the interface.
, in the formation of Schottky barrier, there is a transition from adsorbate-induced gap states to interface metallic character.
the formation of the Schottky barrier on GaAs(100) is determined by the interplay of adsorbate-induced gap states and the formation of interface metallicity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Fermi level pinning at the semiconductor surface can be understood as a consequence of the formation of a metallic-like interface.
the pinning of E _{F} at GaAs(110) is not due to adsorbate-induced gap states, but is due to a metallic interface.

the formation of Schottky barriers on n-type semiconductors involves two distinct stages: the formation of adsorbate induced gap states at low coverage and the onset of interface metallicity at high coverage.
